newsitem.title: USA: Witness tells of secondhand smoke risk in planes.
newsitem.headline: Witness tells of secondhand smoke risk in planes.

text.p: Flight attendants working in smoky aircraft cabins face worse and riskier exposure to cancer-causing secondhand smoke than waiters and bartenders, a public health expert on Friday told jurors hearing a $5 billion anti-tobacco case.

Michael Siegel, a physician and expert on the causes of diseases, testified that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer, emphysema and seven other diseases, as well as aggravating ailments such as respiratory disorders.
"I believe that secondhand smoke exposure in airline cabins caused lung cancer in flight attendants," said Siegel, a professor at the Boston University School of Public Health.

Siegel, whose testimony was repeatedly challenged by tobacco company lawyers, was called as a witness by lawyers pressing a landmark secondhand-smoke case on behalf of an estimated 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants with tobacco-related illnesses such as heart disease.
Other witnesses, including a former U.S. surgeon general, have also said since testimony began on Wednesday that secondhand smoke causes disease.

The tobacco companies fighting the lawsuit deny secondhand smoke is a health risk and say the average non-smoking flight attendant's exposure to secondhand smoke was trivial, before smoking was banned on U.S. airlines in 1988.
Siegel said during questioning by tobacco company lawyers that secondhand smoke was in some ways more dangerous than the fumes taken in by smokers.

"The non-smoker who is inhaling secondhand smoke is tending to inhale much larger amounts of smaller particles that go deep down into the lung, penetrate and can ultimately cause lung cancer," Siegel said.

The author of a 1993 article in the Journal of the American Medical Association on secondhand-smoke risks among restaurant staff, Siegel said servers and bartenders spending eight-hour shifts in smoky places were much more heavily exposed to secondhand smoke than diners and endured three to four times the exposure of a person sharing an office or a home with smokers,
Flight attendants working in enclosed cabins with no fresh air had more secondhand-smoke exposure than food service workers, Siegel said.
Published measurements of secondhand smoke in airliner cabins were about twice the level found in restaurants, he said.

Smoking has been curbed or barred in many offices and public facilities throughout the United States since the mid-1980s, largely because of health worries about secondhand smoke, but is still largely allowed in bars and many restaurants.

Siegel also said during questioning by tobacco lawyers that flight attendants on smoking flights encountered especially dense secondhand smoke because they tended to spend most of their time in galleys and other areas in or near smoking sections.

Edward Moss, an attorney for Brown & Williamson Tobacco, one of the defendants, asked the trial judge to strike Siegel's testimony because a measurement for nicotine levels he gave for secondhand smoke during his testimony did not match the figure he gave during pre-trial questioning by tobacco company lawyers.

Judge Robert Kaye of Dade County Court refused. When questioned on the witness stand by Moss, Siegel said he had erred on the nicotine measurement during the questioning last May but had not altered his data.

Testimony in the case, Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris et al, was scheduled to continue on Monday, when breakaway tobacco executive Bennett LeBow, chairman of Brooke Group, owner of Liggett Group, takes the stand.
Liggett is one of the defendants in the case, but LeBow has become a pariah in the tobacco industry since striking separate deals with anti-tobacco forces in other lawsuits.
Broin is both the first secondhand-smoke case and the first class-action suit against the U.S. tobacco industry to come to trial.
